title: King Ambarisha's senses
hookLine: a king who could have any pleasure gives each of his senses to God, and it's why a puja has a lamp, a bell, incense, flowers and food
carry: master the senses by offering them

cards: You met King Ambarisha on day one thirty, keeping his Ekadashi fast while an angry sage raged. The Bhagavata says he ruled the whole earth. Any pleasure a king could want was his for the asking.
Here's what he did with his senses. His eyes he gave to seeing Vishnu's images. His ears, to hearing Vishnu's stories.
His hands, to cleaning Vishnu's temple. His nose, to the scent of tulsi from Vishnu's feet. And his tongue, to tasting food first offered to God.

teach.b: Ambarisha didn't shut his senses down. He turned them. That's the Hindu teaching about the senses.
The Katha Upanishad calls them horses: strong, and the work is to steer them, not to kill them.
Patanjali calls it indriya-jaya, mastery of the senses. Sutra 3.47: by samyama on the senses in five aspects, mastery.
Not just what you see, but the seeing itself; the sense of me that says I see; and what the senses are for. Sutra 3.48: from that comes a swiftness like the mind, and mastery over nature itself.

One way to read book three: it walks from the outside in. yesterday the elements, what's known; today the senses, the knowing; tomorrow, the one who knows. The devotional path does it Ambarisha's way.

Look at a Hindu puja: a lamp for the eyes, a bell for the ears, incense and flowers for the nose, food offered and shared back as prasad for the tongue, sandal paste and flowers, offered by hand, for touch.
Many teachers read it as every sense brought to God at once.
Now the week. Dattatreya's wasp. Dhruva's steady star.
Hanuman's heart. The walker on water. Shankara in a king's body.
Hanuman's service. And Ambarisha. A week of powers, and every story points past them.

teach.h: MASTER THE SENSES BY OFFERING THEM.
teach.b: Today your senses get pulled all day, by screens built to catch them. Ambarisha's answer isn't to close your eyes. It's to give them something worth seeing.

how: A Hindu puja engages every sense, with lamp, bell, incense, flowers, sandal paste and food offered and received back as prasad; devotional teachers point to King Ambarisha as the model of senses turned toward God, and yoga teachers present 3.47 as samyama on perception itself.

o: a sharper eye and ear from daily exercise
mastery of the senses, by samyama on them
shutting the senses down by sheer willpower

games.q: the senses, turned — tap the pairs.

s: mastery of the senses means numbing them
Ambarisha turned his senses toward God; 3.48 says mastery makes perception swift.
the Bhagavata says Ambarisha gave each sense to Vishnu
eyes to his images, ears to his stories, hands to his temple, tongue to food offered.
book three walks from the known, to the knowing, to the knower
elements, then senses, then tomorrow the one who knows.

games.q: your phone pulls at your eyes and ears all day. what's Ambarisha's way?
o: give the senses something worthy, the way he gave his to God.
switch every sense off and feel nothing.
let them go wherever they're pulled.
games.why: Ambarisha didn't shut his senses down; he turned each one toward Vishnu. that's mastery, not numbness.

practice: If you have a lamp or a candle, light it; if not, picture one. Give it your eyes for a moment. Then your ears: one sound around you.

Then smell, taste and touch: the air, your own mouth, your hands resting. If you pray, offer each sense to God as you go, the way Ambarisha did. If you don't, simply give each one your full attention.

wordCard.voice: Indriya-jaya, mastery of the senses. By samyama on the senses in five aspects, it brings a swiftness like the mind's own.

orig.note: Sanskrit indriya-jaya: mastery (jaya) of the senses (indriya), 3.47.

carryVoice: Your line: master the senses by offering them. Ambarisha turned every one toward God. A week of the powers, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 9.4.15–20 (Ambarisha rules the earth and gives each sense to Vishnu)
Katha Upanishad 1.3.3–4 (the chariot: the senses are the horses)
Yoga Sutra 3.47 (samyama on the senses in five aspects)
Yoga Sutra 3.48 (swiftness like the mind; perception without instruments; mastery of primal nature)
